I've gathered substantial material. Let me now compile the verse-by-verse notes from the sources retrieved. I was unable to reach Catholic, Orthodox, or modern scholarship sites due to search limits, but I have solid coverage across multiple Protestant traditions.

---

## 2 Kings 18 – Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### v. 1 — Hezekiah's Accession

**Traditional Reading:**
Hezekiah ("Yahweh is my strength") became king in the third year of Hoshea of Israel, around 729/728 B.C. as co-regent with his father Ahaz, and later as sole ruler from about 716/715 B.C. His accession came at the very end of the Northern Kingdom — the fall of Samaria was only a few years away, which served as a sobering object lesson for Judah.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-18/
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-18-commentary

John Gill notes this "third year" refers to the third year of Hoshea's rebellion against Assyria, when he stopped paying tribute.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-kings-18.html

**Chronological debate:** Patterson and Austel call the synchronisms in this chapter "perhaps the knottiest of all scriptural chronological problems," noting various attempts at harmonisation remain difficult.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-18/

---

### v. 2 — Age, Reign Length, and Mother

**Traditional Reading:**
Hezekiah was 25 at accession and reigned 29 years in Jerusalem (14 before his illness and 15 after, per Pulpit). His mother's name in Kings is "Abi" (meaning "my father"), but 2 Chronicles 29:1 gives it as "Abijah" ("Jehovah is my father"), which is likely the correct form.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_kings/18.htm
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-18-commentary

**Godly maternal influence:** Several commentators highlight that Hezekiah's mother, daughter of Zechariah (possibly the same Zechariah of Isaiah 8:2), was likely the key to his godliness despite having the notoriously wicked Ahaz as his father. F.B. Meyer says, "It was wonderful that such a father as Ahaz should have had such a son; but he probably had a good mother."
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-18-commentary

**Baptist view (Gill):** Gill discusses the apparent chronological difficulty of Ahaz having a son at age 11, noting that Ahaz may have been nearer 21 at his accession and that begetting children at a young age is not incredible historically.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-kings-18.html

---

### v. 3 — "He Did What Was Right"

**Traditional Reading:**
Hezekiah received the unqualified praise "according to all that David his father did" — a description applied to only two other Judean kings: Asa (1 Kings 15:11) and Josiah (2 Kings 22:2). The Pulpit Commentary observes that all three were curiously sons of wicked fathers. Hezekiah was probably brought under Isaiah's influence at an early age.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_kings/18.htm

**"David redivivus":** Dale Ralph Davis calls Hezekiah "David revived" — after the disastrous reign of Ahaz, it was almost too much to hope for a king who truly followed David's pattern.
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-18-commentary

**Reformed/Presbyterian (G. Campbell Morgan):** Morgan notes, "It is remarkable that such a man as Hezekiah could be the son of Ahaz. Yet we must remember that all his life he was under the influence of Isaiah."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-18/

---

### v. 4 — Removing High Places and the Bronze Serpent

This is one of the richest verses in the chapter.

**The high places:** Hezekiah was the first king who dared to remove the high places — local worship sites that even good kings like Joash, Amaziah, Uzziah, and Jotham had tolerated. As Dilday notes, "God was never happy about this practice, but none of the other good kings ever found the courage to forbid it. Hezekiah did."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-18/

**The bronze serpent (Nehushtan):** The bronze serpent made by Moses (Numbers 21:8–9) had been preserved for about 700–730 years. By Hezekiah's time, the Israelites were burning incense to it as an idol. Hezekiah smashed it and called it "Nehushtan" — meaning "a piece of brass" or "the little brass thing" (a diminutive of contempt).
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_kings/18.htm
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-18-commentary

**Typological significance:** Jesus Himself used the bronze serpent as a type of His crucifixion (John 3:14–15). The Pulpit Commentary argues this is precisely why Moses would have been instructed to preserve it with the tabernacle furniture rather than leaving it in the wilderness. Yet the very thing that once brought healing became an idol needing destruction.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_kings/18.htm

**Baptist view (Spurgeon):** "Although it was an interesting memorial, it must be utterly destroyed, because it presented a temptation to idolatry. Here if ever in this world was a relic of high antiquity, of undoubted authenticity… yet it must be broken in pieces, because Israel burned incense to it."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-18/

**Pentecostal/Charismatic application (Enduring Word / David Guzik):** Good things can become destructive idols and must sometimes be destroyed. If the true cross or Jesus' burial cloth were discovered and became idolatrous distractions, they too should be destroyed. Modern idolatry includes making leaders, education, human eloquence, customs of ministry, or forms of worship into idols.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-18/

**F.B. Meyer (Holiness tradition):** Meyer compares Nehushtan to the crucifix that has become "a kind of fetish" in his own day. Hezekiah's reform "must have raised an immense amount of opposition; but he did not swerve to the right or left."
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-18-commentary

**Archaeological context:** John Walton (OT scholar) notes that serpent figures crafted in copper or bronze have been found throughout the ancient Near East, often as cultic images associated with healing and fertility. Nehushtan fits a well-attested pattern of serpent worship in Syro-Palestine.
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-18-commentary

**Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary:** "This reminds one of the multiplicity of shrines to men and women today, and of sites where some spectacular event occurred. It is possible to allow such things to get far out of hand, when people give reverence to them."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/2-kings-18.html

**Gill (Baptist):** Gill notes that the idolatrous burning of incense to the serpent probably began in the time of Ahaz, not earlier, since Asa and Jehoshaphat would never have tolerated it. He adds a Jewish tradition that Hezekiah ground it to powder and scattered it to the wind.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-kings-18.html

---

### v. 5 — Unmatched Trust

**Traditional Reading:**
Hezekiah's defining quality was trust in Yahweh. Unlike Hoshea (who relied on Egypt) and Ahaz (who relied on Assyria), Hezekiah discarded trust in man and relied wholly on God. The Pulpit Commentary explains that while the same words are used about Josiah (2 Kings 23:25), the pre-eminence differs: Hezekiah excels in *faith/trust*, Josiah in *works/obedience to the Law*. "One excels in faith, the other in works; Josiah's whole life is one of activity, Hezekiah's great merit lies in his being content, in the crisis of his fate, to 'stand still, and see the salvation of God.'"
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_kings/18.htm

**Gill (Baptist):** Gill's Targum note says Hezekiah "trusted in the Word of the Lord God" — the Word, the Son of God, "not in Nehushtan, but in him the brasen serpent was a type of."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-kings-18.html

**MacArthur (Reformed Baptist / GTY):** "The most noble quality of Hezekiah (in dramatic contrast to his father, Ahaz) was that he relied on the Lord as his exclusive hope in every situation."
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-18-commentary

---

### v. 6 — Steadfast Obedience

**Traditional Reading:**
Hezekiah "clung" (Hebrew *dabaq*) to the LORD, the same word used for the marriage bond (Genesis 2:24). He did not depart from following God and kept the commandments given through Moses. The Pulpit Commentary notes that Hezekiah persevered through his whole life, unlike Asa and Uzziah who fell into sin at the end.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_kings/18.htm
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-18-commentary

**F.B. Meyer:** "There is no such way of meeting temptation and danger as by putting the heart right with God. Cleave to Him; depart not from following Him; keep His commandments: so shall the Lord be with you."
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-18-commentary

---

### v. 7 — Prosperity and Rebellion against Assyria

**Traditional Reading:**
"The LORD was with him" — the Pulpit Commentary notes this exact phrase is used of no other king of Judah or Israel except David (2 Samuel 5:10). It was the promise made to Moses, repeated to Joshua, and fulfilled in Hezekiah. His rebellion against Assyria was not sinful but a righteous casting off of the yoke of subjugation that his father Ahaz had wickedly submitted to.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_kings/18.htm
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-18/

**Evangelical note (Enduring Word):** The rebellion at the beginning of Hezekiah's reign (refusing tribute) was justified. Later, Zedekiah's rebellion against Babylon was not — showing that "sometimes rebellion is justified and sometimes it is not."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-18/

**Bridgeway Bible Commentary:** Hezekiah's revolt came after he was assured of military support from Egypt. Isaiah opposed this reliance on Egypt, insisting what Judah needed was "not military help from Egypt but quiet faith in God" (Isaiah 30:1-3, 15).
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bbc/2-kings-18.html

---

### v. 8 — Victory over the Philistines

**Traditional Reading:**
Hezekiah subdued the Philistines all the way to Gaza, recovering territory lost during his father Ahaz's reign (2 Chronicles 28:18). The phrase "from the watchtower to the fortified city" is a proverbial expression meaning every kind of settlement, from the smallest outpost to the largest walled city.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-kings-18.html
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_kings/18.htm

The Pulpit Commentary adds that Hezekiah's Philistine war was part of a broader anti-Assyrian league involving Philistia, Judah, Edom, and Moab. Hezekiah attacked Assyrian partisans among the Philistines.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_kings/18.htm

---

### vv. 9–12 — The Fall of Samaria Recounted

**Traditional Reading:**
These verses briefly recount the fall of the Northern Kingdom (already narrated in detail in 2 Kings 17). Shalmaneser besieged Samaria starting in Hezekiah's 4th year (Hoshea's 7th); it fell after three years in Hezekiah's 6th year. The Israelites were exiled to Halah, Gozan by the Habor River, and cities of the Medes.
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-18-commentary

The Pulpit Commentary raises the question of who actually took Samaria: the plural verb "they took it" (Hebrew *yilk'duha*) suggests the writer knew Shalmaneser died during the siege and the capture fell to his successor Sargon II.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_kings/18.htm

**Theological purpose:** The fall of Israel is recounted here as a deliberate contrast with Hezekiah's faithfulness and as a warning to Judah. The reason is explicit: "because they did not listen to the voice of the LORD their God, but violated His covenant."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-18/
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bbc/2-kings-18.html

---

### v. 13 — Sennacherib's Invasion

**Traditional Reading:**
"In the fourteenth year of King Hezekiah" (c. 701 B.C.), Sennacherib of Assyria attacked and captured all the fortified cities of Judah. This was about 20 years after the fall of Samaria.

**Historical-critical note (Pulpit Commentary):** The Pulpit Commentary openly challenges the "fourteenth year" date as irreconcilable with the Assyrian inscriptions, which place Sennacherib's accession in 705 B.C. and his first campaign against Hezekiah in his 4th year (701 B.C.). The Pulpit suggests the date was inserted later by a redactor who assumed the events of 2 Kings 20:6 belonged to the time of Sennacherib's attack. However, Sennacherib's own annals confirm his attack on Judah, claiming he captured 46 fortified cities.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_kings/18.htm

**Archaeological note:** The British Museum displays Assyrian reliefs depicting Sennacherib's siege of Lachish, an important fortress city about 30 miles southwest of Jerusalem. Archaeologists also discovered a pit at Lachish with about 1,500 casualties, though those likely came from Nebuchadnezzar's later attack.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-18/

---

### vv. 14–16 — Hezekiah's Tribute to Sennacherib

**Traditional Reading:**
Hezekiah, seeing all his fortified cities captured, lost heart and sent to Sennacherib at Lachish saying, "I have done wrong; withdraw from me, and I will pay whatever you demand." Sennacherib imposed 300 talents of silver and 30 talents of gold. Hezekiah paid by emptying the temple treasuries and the royal palace, and even stripped the gold plating from the temple doors and doorposts that he himself had overlaid.

**Enduring Word (Guzik):** This was "a clear — though understandable — lack of faith." Hezekiah felt it wiser to pay off Assyria than to trust God. The policy of appeasement "only impoverished Judah and the temple and made the king of Assyria more bold than ever against Judah."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-18/

**Pulpit Commentary:** Ahaz had already exhausted the temple treasuries about 30 years earlier (2 Kings 16:8), so there wasn't much accumulation. Hence the stripping of gold plating. The Pulpit also notes from Sennacherib's inscriptions that Hezekiah's submission included ceding territory, surrendering a vassal king he was harbouring, and contributing daughters to the Assyrian harem at Nineveh.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_kings/18.htm

**Gill:** Gill also references the Talmudic rabbis who list this as one of "the three things the Talmudic writers disapprove of in Hezekiah."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-kings-18.html

**Bridgeway:** Hezekiah at first prepared Jerusalem's defences and encouraged the people to trust God (2 Chronicles 32:1-8), but "on seeing the strength of the siege, Hezekiah began to repent of his rebellion and offered to pay whatever money Sennacherib demanded."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bbc/2-kings-18.html

---

### vv. 17–18 — The Assyrian Envoys Arrive

**Traditional Reading:**
Despite receiving the tribute, Sennacherib sent the Tartan (commander-in-chief), the Rabsaris (chief eunuch/officer), and the Rabshakeh (field commander, possibly originally "chief cup-bearer") with a great army to Jerusalem. They stationed themselves at the aqueduct of the upper pool on the road to the Launderer's Field — the very place where Isaiah had confronted Ahaz (Isaiah 7:3). Three Judean officials came out: Eliakim (palace administrator, replacing the disgraced Shebna — see Isaiah 22:15-25), Shebna (now demoted to scribe), and Joah (the recorder).
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-18/
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_kings/18.htm

**Enduring Word:** The choice of location was strategic — the aqueduct at the upper pool was Jerusalem's crucial water supply, its lifeline in a siege. The Rabshakeh standing there demonstrated complete Assyrian command of the situation.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-18/

---

### vv. 19–20 — The Rabshakeh's Opening Challenge

**Traditional Reading:**
The Rabshakeh asked, "What is the basis of this confidence of yours? You claim to have strategy and strength for war, but these are empty words. In whom are you now trusting, that you have rebelled against me?"

**Enduring Word:** The Rabshakeh was targeting Hezekiah's trust in his Egyptian alliance, not his trust in Yahweh. It was a valid question from an unbeliever's perspective. F.B. Meyer is quoted: "Our life must to a large extent be a mystery, our peace pass understanding, and our motives be hidden. The sources of our supply, the ground of our confidence, the reasons for our actions, must evade the most searching scrutiny of those who stand outside the charmed circle of the face of God."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-18/

---

### vv. 21–25 — The Rabshakeh's Four Arguments

**Traditional Reading:**

**(1) v. 21 — Egypt is a "splintered reed":** Leaning on Egypt is like leaning on a broken reed that pierces the hand. Ironically, Isaiah had used the same image (Isaiah 30:1-7; 31:1-3). The Rabshakeh could see Egypt's weakness better than many Judean leaders.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-18/

**(2) v. 22 — Hezekiah's reforms have offended Yahweh:** The Rabshakeh misunderstood (perhaps deliberately) the centralisation of worship, arguing that removing the high places had angered the God of Israel. Grogan (Isaiah commentary) notes this "theological misunderstanding" actually argues for the speech's authenticity rather than it being a free creation by the author.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-18/

**(3) vv. 23–24 — Judah's military weakness:** The Rabshakeh mocked Judah's army by offering 2,000 horses if Judah could find riders, then pointed out they couldn't repel even a single Assyrian junior officer.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-18/

**(4) v. 25 — Yahweh sent me:** The Rabshakeh claimed, "The LORD Himself said to me, 'Go up against this land and destroy it.'" Dilday suggests Sennacherib may have been familiar with Isaiah's prophecies that Assyria was the rod of Yahweh's anger (Isaiah 10:5), and used this to demoralise Judah.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-18/

**Enduring Word's spiritual application:** "Satan often tries to talk us into surrender rather than fight us directly... The enemy of our soul uses the exact same approach... He would much rather try to talk you into giving up!" This is compared to Satan's temptation of Jesus in the wilderness (Luke 4:5-8).
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-18/

---

### vv. 26–27 — "Speak in Aramaic!"

**Traditional Reading:**
The Judean officials begged the Rabshakeh to speak in Aramaic (the diplomatic language of the Near East) rather than Hebrew (Judahite), so the common people listening on the wall wouldn't understand. The Rabshakeh cruelly refused, shouting that his message was for everyone — those doomed "to eat their own dung and drink their own urine" (the horrific conditions of a prolonged siege).
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-18/
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bbc/2-kings-18.html

---

### vv. 28–35 — The Rabshakeh's Direct Appeal to the People

**Traditional Reading:**

The Rabshakeh stood and shouted in Hebrew directly to the people on the wall, delivering a three-part appeal:

**(1) vv. 29–30 — Don't trust Hezekiah or his God:** "Do not let Hezekiah deceive you; he cannot deliver you from my hand. Do not let Hezekiah persuade you to trust in the LORD."

**(2) vv. 31–32 — Surrender and enjoy peace — then exile:** "Make peace with me and come out to me. Then every one of you will eat from his own vine and his own fig tree... until I come and take you away to a land like your own." This was the classic Assyrian deportation policy, dressed up as benevolence: "a land of grain and new wine, a land of bread and vineyards, a land of olive trees and honey."

**(3) vv. 33–35 — No god has ever withstood Assyria:** The Rabshakeh listed conquered cities — Hamath, Arpad, Sepharvaim, Hena, Ivvah, and Samaria — and argued that since their gods couldn't save them, neither could Yahweh save Jerusalem. This was the fatal theological error: equating Yahweh with the powerless idols of the nations.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-18/
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bbc/2-kings-18.html

**Bridgeway Bible Commentary:** "Their big mistake, however, was to insult Yahweh by claiming he was no stronger than the gods of other nations whom the Assyrians had conquered."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bbc/2-kings-18.html

---

### vv. 36–37 — The People's Silence and the Officials' Grief

**Traditional Reading:**
The people obeyed Hezekiah's command and remained completely silent — they "did not answer a word." Then Eliakim, Shebna, and Joah returned to Hezekiah with their clothes torn (a sign of deep mourning and distress) and reported the Rabshakeh's words.

**Enduring Word (Guzik):** The people's silence was wise. "Often, it is useless — if not dangerous — to try and match wits with demonic logic. Instead, it is better to stay silent and trust God."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-18/

**John Piper (Reformed Baptist — Desiring God):** Although Piper's sermon focuses on the prayer in chapter 19, he emphasises that Hezekiah's response to the crisis was to go to the house of the Lord and spread the matter before God. "He did not assume prayer was redundant or unnecessary. Rather, he assumed that his prayers really mattered — that God meant to win this war through prayer."
— https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/winning-battles-through-prayer
— https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/what-difference-will-prayer-make

### Summary of Distinctive Protestant Theological Emphases

| Tradition | Distinctive Emphasis |
|-----------|---------------------|
| **Reformed/Presbyterian** (Pulpit, Morgan) | Hezekiah's faith vs. Josiah's works distinction; God's sovereignty in using Assyria as rod of judgment |
| **Baptist** (Spurgeon, Gill, Garner-Howes) | Nehushtan as warning against relic-veneration; trust in the "Word of the Lord" (Christ); believer's baptism parallel of destroying old idols |
| **Pentecostal/Charismatic** (Enduring Word/Guzik) | Spiritual warfare emphasis — Rabshakeh as Satan-like deceiver; practical application of destroying modern idols (leaders, education, forms of worship) |
| **Holiness/Methodist** (F.B. Meyer) | Nehushtan compared to crucifix as fetish; moral reform as preparation for battle; "cleave to Him, depart not" |
| **Reformed Baptist** (Piper, MacArthur) | Prayer as divinely ordained means; God's "all-embracing, invincible sovereignty" operating through Hezekiah's trust |
